+#' Run validated calculations and export provisional CSV/PNG review artefacts.
+#'
+#' This entry point cannot grant official acceptance. Prior run directories are
+#' never overwritten; calculation/export failures mark this run as failed.
+run_population_analysis <- function(project_root, config_file = "config/ons_rm121_2021.yml") {
+  functions <- new.env(parent = globalenv())
+  code_files <- c("configuration.R", "ingestion.R", "validation.R", "category_mapping.R",
+                  "summarisation.R", "presentation.R")
+  for (file in code_files) sys.source(file.path(project_root, "R", file), envir = functions)
+  checkpoint <- new.env(parent = globalenv())
+  sys.source(file.path(project_root, "scripts", "validate_population_input.R"), envir = checkpoint)
+  validated <- checkpoint$run_input_validation(project_root, config_file)
+  run_path <- validated$run_directory
+  manifest_path <- file.path(run_path, "manifest.json")
+  manifest <- jsonlite::read_json(manifest_path, simplifyVector = FALSE)
+  manifest$stage <- "population_analysis"
+  manifest$status <- "calculations_in_progress"
+  save_manifest <- function() jsonlite::write_json(manifest, manifest_path, auto_unbox = TRUE, pretty = TRUE, null = "null")
+  save_manifest()
+  tryCatch({
+    config <- functions$read_population_config(project_root, config_file)
+    references <- functions$read_population_references(config)
+    mapped <- functions$derive_population_age_groups(validated$data, references$age)
+    group_keys <- c("sex_code", "sex_label", "age_group", "age_group_order")
+    denominator_keys <- c("sex_code", "sex_label")
+    totals <- functions$aggregate_population(
+      mapped, group_keys, c("geography_code", "sex_code", "source_age_code")
+    )
+    results <- functions$calculate_population_percentages(
+      totals, group_keys, denominator_keys, config$analysis$percentage_tolerance
+    )
+    if (nrow(results) != nrow(references$sex) * dplyr::n_distinct(references$age$age_group)) {
+      stop("Unexpected number of reporting groups.", call. = FALSE)
+    }
+    # Compare pre-aggregation sex totals with the final denominator table.
+    source_totals <- validated$data |>
+      dplyr::group_by(sex_code, sex_label) |>
+      dplyr::summarise(expected = sum(population), .groups = "drop")
+    reconciled <- results |>
+      dplyr::distinct(sex_code, sex_label, denominator_population) |>
+      dplyr::left_join(source_totals, by = denominator_keys, relationship = "one-to-one")
+    if (anyNA(reconciled$expected) || any(reconciled$expected != reconciled$denominator_population)) {
+      stop("Within-sex totals changed during processing.", call. = FALSE)
+    }
+    review <- functions$prepare_population_review(results, config)
+    review_path <- file.path(run_path, "review")
+    if (!dir.create(review_path)) stop("Cannot create review-output directory.", call. = FALSE)
+    csv_path <- file.path(review_path, "provisional_population_by_age_sex.csv")
+    png_path <- file.path(review_path, "provisional_population_by_age_sex.png")
+    readr::write_csv(review, csv_path)
+    ggplot2::ggsave(png_path, plot = functions$population_review_chart(review, config),
+                    width = 11, height = 7, units = "in", dpi = 150)
+    checks <- dplyr::bind_rows(validated$checks, tibble::tibble(
+      check_id = c("P0-11", "P0-13", "P0-14", "P0-17"), status = "pass",
+      detail = c("Exact age mapping preserves records and counts", "Overall and within-sex totals reconcile",
+                 "Positive denominators and unrounded percentages reconcile", "Explicit chronological category order")
+    ))
+    readr::write_csv(checks, file.path(run_path, "validation_checks.csv"))
+    manifest$status <- "provisional_review_outputs_created_not_officially_validated"
+    manifest$official_acceptance <- "blocked"
+    manifest$group_keys <- group_keys
+    manifest$denominator_keys <- denominator_keys
+    manifest$total_population <- functions$safe_population_total(review$population)
+    manifest$result_rows <- nrow(review)
+    manifest$finished_utc <- format(Sys.time(), tz = "UTC", usetz = TRUE)
+    tracked_code <- c(stats::setNames(file.path(config$project_root, "R", code_files), code_files),
+                      analysis_runner = file.path(config$project_root, "scripts", "run_population_analysis.R"))
+    manifest$analysis_code_sha256 <- lapply(tracked_code, function(path) digest::digest(file = path, algo = "sha256"))
+    tracked_outputs <- c(results = csv_path, chart = png_path,
+                         validation = file.path(run_path, "validation_checks.csv"))
+    manifest$output_sha256 <- lapply(tracked_outputs, function(path) digest::digest(file = path, algo = "sha256"))
+    save_manifest()
+    invisible(list(results = review, checks = checks, run_directory = run_path, csv = csv_path, chart = png_path))
+  }, error = function(error) {
+    manifest$status <- "failed"
+    manifest$error <- conditionMessage(error)
+    manifest$finished_utc <- format(Sys.time(), tz = "UTC", usetz = TRUE)
+    save_manifest()
+    stop(error)
+  })

+# Methodology and current limits
+
+This workflow preserves the reviewed SAS calculation, not its known defects.
+Source counts represent authority–sex–age observations. The original text is
+retained during ingestion; invalid records cause failure, not silent exclusion.
+The category references are transcriptions of the supplied extract, not externally
+authenticated ONS codebooks.
+
+Age codes 1–2 map to 0–4, 3–6 to 5–15, 7–9 to 16–24, 10–17 to 25–64,
+and 18–23 to 65+. These are exact unions of source categories. No estimation or
+splitting of counts is performed. Every mapping must be many-to-one and complete.
+
+Counts are summed across observed authorities within each sex and reporting age
+group. A percentage is 100 times the group count divided by the sum across all
+five groups for the same sex. The machine-readable result retains the denominator
+and full-precision percentage. Round to one decimal place only when displaying;
+the rounded male percentages total 100.1%, which is an expected rounding effect.
+
+The supplied-file regression expectations are female 30,420,281, male 29,177,325
+and combined 59,597,606. All ten reviewed group counts are in
+`tests/expected/ons_rm121_2021_results.csv`. These expectations are tied to the
+source checksum in the tests. They are not independently verified official totals.
+
+CSV and PNG outputs are explicitly provisional and remain inside a run-specific
+`review/` directory. The count chart uses separate sex panels with a shared
+scale, so colour is not needed to identify sex. The age groups have unequal widths
+and 65+ is open-ended; the bars are totals, not densities or counts per year of age.
+
+Geography coverage is checked only within observed authorities. No authoritative
+geography list or comparable official benchmark has been supplied, so independent
+coverage and official acceptance remain blocked. The geographical scope and year
+are descriptions inherited from the supplied files, not external certification.
+The workflow cannot promote itself to official acceptance by editing a status flag.
+
+Future adapters must validate their own source schemas and domains. Exact mappings
+must respect classification boundaries. Source and grouping keys must retain
+periods and other context that define separate populations. Do not sum snapshots,
+overlapping geography levels, incompatible classifications, rates or percentages.

 # AI-PoC
+
+## Population-processing workflow
+
+The R workflow replaces the reviewed SAS calculation with explicit ingestion,
+validation, exact age mapping, aggregation and within-sex percentages. The
+original files in [Inputs](Inputs/) are preserved unchanged.
+
+**Current outputs are provisional review artefacts, not accepted official totals.**
+Only the supplied files are available; authoritative geography coverage and
+official benchmark reconciliation remain blocked.
+
+### Running
+
+Use R with readr, dplyr, tidyr, ggplot2, yaml, digest and jsonlite installed. Tests
+also require testthat. Dependency locking and clean-session verification are
+planned; the existing session is not replaced or restarted automatically.
+

+then call `run_population_analysis(project_root)` with the explicit absolute
+project-root path. It returns results and output paths invisibly. Input locations,
+schema and settings are in [config/ons_rm121_2021.yml](config/ons_rm121_2021.yml).
+Paths in configuration are relative to the supplied project root, never a
+personal home directory. No processing step changes the working directory.
+
+Each run creates a new local `outputs/` directory containing validation checks,
+record accounting, session information and a manifest. A successful provisional
+run also contains a `review/` directory with a CSV and PNG. Failed runs are marked
+failed in the manifest; do not use partial artefacts from a failed run. Generated
+outputs are ignored by version control by default, not deleted.
+
+To run ingestion/validation alone, source
+[scripts/validate_population_input.R](scripts/validate_population_input.R) and
+call `run_input_validation(project_root)`.
+
+### Tests and interpretation
+
+From the project root, set `PA_TEST_SCRATCH` to an existing writable scratch
+directory, then run `testthat::test_dir("tests/testthat")`. Test fixtures are
+written only to that scratch directory. Never use the source directory as scratch.
+
+See [methodology](docs/methodology.md) for the denominator, age mapping, rounding
+and interpretation limits, and [implementation progress](docs/implementation_progress.md)
+for agreed decisions and remaining acceptance work.

## Findings

1. **Misleading chronology pass.** `R/ingestion.R:77–81` checks only that age-group orders are unique and finite. Swapping the orders of `0-4` and `65+` would still pass, produce a wrongly ordered chart and CSV, and report “Explicit chronological category order” as passed (`scripts/run_population_analysis.R:61–65`). The tests check the supplied mapping, but the runner does not enforce it.

2. **Percentages can pool periods silently in reuse.** `R/summarisation.R:51–75` permits a caller to omit `period` from denominator keys even when it is in the group keys. The resulting percentages pool periods and still pass the 100% reconciliation. The reuse test supplies the correct denominator but does not test this omission (`tests/testthat/test-calculations.R:61–72`).

3. **Manifest hashes may not identify the rules used.** The validation stage hashes configuration and references before reading them (`scripts/validate_population_input.R:23–31, 37–40`), then the analysis stage rereads both without verifying those hashes (`scripts/run_population_analysis.R:29–31`). An intervening edit can change the mapping or presentation while the manifest records the earlier files.

4. **Some failed runs are not marked failed.** Run-directory creation, hashing, session capture and the initial manifest write occur outside the validation error handler (`scripts/validate_population_input.R:21–37`). A failure there can leave a run directory without a failed manifest. The analysis-stage manifest read and initial update are also outside its handler (`scripts/run_population_analysis.R:21–28`).

The supplied configuration and output code keep official coverage, benchmark reconciliation and acceptance blocked. This was a read-only review; nothing was executed.

# Positron IDE commands

These commands act on the Positron workbench itself -- layout, panes, editors,
interpreter sessions, and packages. They do not run interpreter code; use the
tool that runs code in a session for that.

## Calling these commands

Invoke commands with the tool that runs Positron commands, passing the command's
literal `id` exactly as written in the reference files -- copy it, do not retype
it from memory. Where a command takes arguments, fill `args` positionally in the
order given under that command's "Arguments" entry. Omit `args` entirely for commands
that take none -- do not pass an empty object or array. Never invent an argument
value the user hasn't given you or that isn't documented; if a required value is
unknown, ask the user first.

**Find the id here before you run it.** Positron is built on VS Code, so a
plausible-sounding VS Code command id usually does exist and will usually run --
which makes recalling one from memory the most expensive mistake available. Some
ids that read like they do the thing directly instead open a dialog or a
quick-pick and wait for the user to choose, so the command "succeeds" while
handing the task straight back to them. Read the relevant reference file first
and use the id and arguments it gives you. If what the user wants is not covered
by any file below, say so rather than reaching for an id from general VS Code

These are opaque handles you pass back into another command; they are not shown
anywhere in the Positron UI, so a user won't recognize one and it would only
confuse them. Use ids to make the call, but never repeat one to the user. Refer
to a session or interpreter by its name instead.

1	# Positron package commands
2	
3	Reading, installing and updating the packages in an interpreter session. See
4	[SKILL.md](/Users/alex/Library/Application Support/Positron/User/globalStorage/positron.positron-skills/skills/positron-commands/SKILL.md) for how to call these commands and how to
5	handle failures.
6	
7	The **Arguments** and **Returns** entries below are generated from the running
8	build's command metadata, so they always match this Positron. The surrounding
9	guidance is hand-written.
10	
11	## Read the environment, never probe it
12	
13	To find out what is installed, what version it is, or whether something newer
14	is available, call `positronPackages.getAllPackages` (the whole environment) or
15	`positronPackages.getPackages` (specific packages, by name). **Do not run code
16	to find out.** Writing `import pandas` in a try/except, calling `pip list`,
17	`installed.packages()`, `importlib.metadata.version()`, or anything similar
18	through `executeCode` is the wrong move every time: it runs code the user did
19	not ask for, it can have side effects (an import executes module-level code),
20	it only answers for the one package you thought to test, and it tells you
21	nothing about whether a newer version exists.
22	
23	These commands have none of those problems. They change nothing, show the user
24	nothing, and need no pane open. Reach for one before any package operation, and
25	before answering any question about what the session has.
26	
27	**Which of the two to call:**
28	
29	- To size up the environment, or list what is installed, call
30	  `getAllPackages`. It returns a compact entry per package, built to fit
31	  hundreds of packages at once.
32	- To look a package (or a few) up by name -- its full detail, its security
33	  vulnerabilities, or simply *whether it is installed at all* -- call
34	  `getPackages` with the names. A named package that is missing comes back in
35	  `notFound`, which is a definitive "not installed"; the compact list can be
36	  large, so do not conclude a package is absent just because you did not spot
37	  it there.
38	
39	## Reading what's installed
40	
41	### `positronPackages.getAllPackages`
42	
43	Reports every package installed in the foreground session, each with its
44	installed version and whether a newer one is available. A **compact** list: the
45	`description` is shortened to 256 characters (suffixed with `...` when cut), and
46	security vulnerabilities and the per-package detail fields (license, author,
47	source repository, publication date) are left out entirely to keep the whole
48	environment inside the token budget. When you need the full description, the
49	detail fields, or the vulnerabilities for a package, call `getPackages` with its
50	name.
51	
52	Read-only and quiet. Unlike the write commands below, this has **no
53	precondition** -- it is always callable, and tells you in its payload when it
54	has nothing to say. So a `disabled` failure from a write command does not mean
55	you cannot read.
56	
57	**Reading the payload:**
58	
59	- `available: false` comes with a `reason`, and each one calls for a different
60	  response:
61	  - `disabled` -- the user turned the Packages pane off in settings. Say so;
62	    do not offer to turn it on by running code.
63	  - `no-session` -- nothing is running, so there is no environment to
64	    describe. Ask the user to start an interpreter.
65	  - `session-not-ready` -- a session is starting up (or has exited). This one
66	    is worth retrying shortly; the others are not.
67	  - `unsupported` -- this runtime has no package manager. Nothing here will
68	    work for it.
69	  - `failed` -- the read itself failed; relay `message` rather than guessing.
70	- `metadataStatus` says how far `outdated` can be trusted. Only `fresh` means
71	  the repositories were queried just now. On `cached`, `timed-out` or
72	  `fetch-failed`, report update information as possibly stale rather than
73	  telling the user they are up to date. On `unsupported`, no package has
74	  `outdated` at all, so its absence means nothing.
75	- `session` names the session the answer describes. It is one session's
76	  environment, not the machine's -- do not carry an answer across a session
77	  switch or apply it to a different language.
78	- `attached` is not the same as installed. A package can be installed but not
79	  attached (not `library()`d in R, not imported in Python). "Is pandas
80	  available?" is answered by the package appearing in the list at all;
81	  `attached` only says whether it is on the search path right now.
82	
83	**Arguments:** None.
84	
85	**Returns:** An object with available: true, the session the packages belong to, the installed packages (name, version, latestVersion, outdated, attached, description, url) -- where description is shortened to 256 characters and suffixed with "..." when cut -- and metadataStatus saying how the outdated state was obtained: 'fresh' (repositories queried now), 'cached' (as of the last fetch), 'unsupported' (this runtime reports no outdated state, so no package has it), 'timed-out' (the list is complete but outdated state may be missing), or 'fetch-failed' (the repository query errored; the list is complete, outdated state is whatever an earlier fetch cached). This list carries no security vulnerabilities and no per-package detail; call positronPackages.getPackages for those. When there are no packages to report, an object with available: false and a reason of 'disabled', 'no-session', 'session-not-ready', 'unsupported', or 'failed' -- the last of which also carries a message.
86	
87	### `positronPackages.getPackages`
88	
89	Reports **full detail** on the packages you name: the full description plus the
90	detail fields (license, author, source repository, publication date) and the
91	security vulnerabilities that `getAllPackages` leaves out. Pass an array of
92	names (matching is case-insensitive). Use it to look a package up rather than
93	scanning the whole list, and to answer "is X installed?" reliably.
94	
95	**Reading the payload:**
96	
97	- `packages` holds the named packages that **are** installed, with full detail.
98	- `notFound` holds the names that are **not** installed. A name here is a
99	  definitive "not installed" -- that is the reason to name packages rather than
100	  to search the compact list, which can be large.
101	- `metadataStatus` and `vulnerabilityStatus` mean the same as elsewhere (see
102	  above and the advisories section below).
103	- The same `available: false` reasons apply. In addition, if you call it
104	  without any names it returns `reason: 'no-names'` -- pass the package names.
105	
106	**Arguments:**
107	- `names` (array of string): The package names to look up, as the package repository knows them (for example: dplyr, pandas). Pass an array of names, or a single name. Matching is case-insensitive.
108	
109	**Returns:** An object with available: true, the session the packages belong to, packages (the named packages that are installed, with full detail), notFound (the named packages that are not installed -- a name here is a definitive "not installed", not a truncated-away answer), metadataStatus (how the outdated state was obtained: 'fresh', 'cached', 'unsupported', 'timed-out', or 'fetch-failed'), and vulnerabilityStatus (how advisories were obtained). Each installed package carries name, version, latestVersion, outdated, attached, description, url, license, author, sourceRepository, publishedDate, title, and vulnerabilities. vulnerabilities are the security advisories against the installed version, worst first (id, osvId, score, scoreVersion, severity of 'critical'/'high'/'medium'/'low'/'unscored', summary, fixedIn, published, url); an empty array means the repository was asked and reports nothing against that version, which is an all-clear, while an absent field means there is no advisory data for that package at all, which is not. vulnerabilityStatus says how the advisories were obtained: 'fresh' (Package Manager queried now), 'cached' (the cached advisories were still current), 'disabled' (advisory lookups are turned off in settings), 'unavailable' (a lookup ran and produced nothing, which is not worth retrying), or 'timed-out' (the lookup ran out of time partway). vulnerabilitySource names the Package Manager host that served them and when it answered. When no packages are named, an object with available: false and reason 'no-names'. When there are no packages to report at all, an object with available: false and a reason of 'disabled', 'no-session', 'session-not-ready', 'unsupported', or 'failed' -- the last of which also carries a message.

97	- `package` (string): Package containing the topic (for example: dplyr). Optional; when omitted, all installed packages are searched (R) or the topic is resolved as an import path (Python).
98	
99	**Returns:** An object with found, languageId, topic, package, content, and message. When found is true, content is the help page as Markdown, and topic and package identify the page that was read. When found is false, message explains why (no topic provided, no session for the language, topic not found, or a lookup error).
100	
101	### `positron.help.listPackageDocs`
102	
103	Lists the documentation for an installed package: its help topics (with titles)
104	and its vignettes, the long-form guides that explain a package's workflow. Use
105	it to get oriented in a package you don't know, especially a private or internal
106	one, or when you need a help topic or vignette name you can't guess. For R,
107	each topic's `aliases` are the function names it documents; pass one of those
108	with `package` to `positron.help.readHelpTopic`. For Python, topics are the
109	package's public members, given as full import paths, and the README is the only
110	vignette.
111	
112	**Arguments:**
113	- `package` (string): Name of the package (for example: dplyr or pandas).
114	- `languageId` (string): Language of the package or topic, such as r or python. Defaults to the language of the foreground interpreter session.
115	
116	**Returns:** An object with found, languageId, package, topics, vignettes, and message. When found is true, topics lists help topics (topic, title, and for R, aliases naming the functions the topic documents) and vignettes lists vignettes (name and title). When found is false, message explains why (no package provided, no session for the language, package not installed, or a lookup error).
117	
118	### `positron.help.readVignette`
119	
120	Reads a vignette and returns it as Markdown. Vignette names are not guessable,
121	so get them from `positron.help.listPackageDocs` first. Read a vignette when the
122	user wants to learn how to use a package or asks about its intended workflow,
123	rather than about a single function. Vignettes can be long, so read one only
124	when it is relevant to the question.
125	
126	**Arguments:**
127	- `package` (string): Name of the package (for example: dplyr).
128	- `vignette` (string): Name of the vignette, as listed by positron.help.listPackageDocs (for example: colwise).
129	- `languageId` (string): Language of the package or topic, such as r or python. Defaults to the language of the foreground interpreter session.
130	
131	**Returns:** An object with found, languageId, package, vignette, title, content, and message. When found is true, content is the vignette as Markdown (or its source, for vignettes without HTML output). When found is false, message explains why (missing arguments, no session for the language, vignette not found, or a lookup error).

Result: {"found":true,"languageId":"r","topic":"snapshot","package":"renv","content":" ### Record current state of the project library in the lockfile #### Description Call `renv::snapshot()` to update a lockfile with the current state of dependencies in the project library. The lockfile can be used to later restore these dependencies as required. It's also possible to call `renv::snapshot()` with a non-renv project, in which case it will record the current state of dependencies in the current library paths. This makes it possible to restore the current packages, providing lightweight portability and reproducibility without isolation. If you want to automatically snapshot after each change, you can set `config$config$auto.snapshot(TRUE)` – see `?config` for more details. #### Usage ``` R snapshot( project = NULL, ..., library = NULL, lockfile = paths$lockfile(project = project), type = settings$snapshot.type(project = project), dev = NULL, repos = getOption("repos"), packages = NULL, exclude = NULL, prompt = interactive(), update = FALSE, force = FALSE, reprex = FALSE, description = NULL ) ``` #### Arguments
project

The project directory. If NULL, then the active project will be used. If no project is currently active, then the current working directory is used instead.
...

Unused arguments, reserved for future expansion. If any arguments are matched to ..., renv will signal an error.
library

The R libraries to snapshot. When NULL, the active R libraries (as reported by .libPaths()) are used.
lockfile

The location where the generated lockfile should be written. By default, the lockfile is written to a file called renv.lock in the project directory. When NULL, the lockfile (as an R object) is returned directly instead.
type

The type of snapshot to perform:

  • "implicit", (the default), uses all packages captured by dependencies().

  • "explicit" uses packages recorded in DESCRIPTION.

  • "all" uses all packages in the project library.

  • "custom" uses a custom filter.

See Snapshot types below for more details.
dev

Boolean; include development dependencies? These packages are typically required when developing the project, but not when running it (i.e. you want them installed when humans are working on the project but not when computers are deploying it).

Development dependencies include packages listed in the Suggests field of a DESCRIPTION found in the project root, and roxygen2 or devtools if their use is implied by other project metadata. They also include packages used in ⁠~/.Rprofile⁠ if config$user.profile() is TRUE.
repos

The R repositories to be recorded in the lockfile. Defaults to the currently active package repositories, as retrieved by getOption("repos").
packages

A vector of packages to be included in the lockfile. When NULL (the default), all packages relevant for the type of snapshot being performed will be included. When set, the type argument is ignored. Recursive dependencies of the specified packages will be added to the lockfile as well.
exclude

A vector of packages to be explicitly excluded from the lockfile. Note that transitive package dependencies will always be included, to avoid potentially creating an incomplete / non-functional lockfile.
prompt

Boolean; prompt the user before taking any action? For backwards compatibility, confirm is accepted as an alias for prompt.
update

Boolean; if the lockfile already exists, then attempt to update that lockfile without removing any prior package records.
force

Boolean; force generation of a lockfile even when pre-flight validation checks have failed?
reprex

Boolean; generate output appropriate for embedding the lockfile as part of a reprex?
description

A package DESCRIPTION, provided either as a named list of DESCRIPTION fields, or a path to a package directory or DESCRIPTION file. When set, all other arguments are ignored, and a single lockfile record for that package is returned.
#### Value The generated lockfile, as an **R** object (invisibly). Note that this function is normally called for its side effects. When `description` is provided, a single lockfile record (a named list) is returned instead. #### Snapshot types Depending on how you prefer to manage your **R** package dependencies, you may want to enable an alternate snapshot type.. The types available are as follows: `"implicit"` (The default) Capture only packages which appear to be used in your project, as determined by `renv::dependencies()`. This ensures that only the packages actually required by your project will enter the lockfile; the downside if it might be slow if your project contains a large number of files. If speed becomes an issue, you might consider using `.renvignore` files to limit which files renv uses for dependency discovery, or switching to explicit mode, as described next. `"explicit"` Only capture packages which are explicitly listed in the project `DESCRIPTION` file. This workflow is recommended for users who wish to manage their project's **R** package dependencies directly, and can be used for both package and non-package **R** projects. Packages used in this manner should be recorded in either the `Depends` or `Imports` field of the `DESCRIPTION` file. `"all"` Capture all packages within the active **R** libraries in the lockfile. This is the quickest and simplest method, but may lead to undesired packages (e.g. development dependencies) entering the lockfile. `"custom"` Like `"implicit"`, but use a custom user-defined filter instead. The filter should be specified by the **R** option `renv.snapshot.filter`, and should either be a character vector naming a function (e.g. `"package::method"`), or be a function itself. The function should only accept one argument (the project directory), and should return a vector of package names to include in the lockfile. You can change the snapshot type for the current project with `settings()`. For example, the following code will switch to using `"explicit"` snapshots: renv::settings$snapshot.type("explicit") When the `packages` argument is set, `type` is ignored, and instead only the requested set of packages, and their recursive dependencies, will be written to the lockfile. #### Package projects When snapshotting a package project (that is, a project containing a `DESCRIPTION` file), renv normally records only the package's dependencies in the lockfile, and excludes the package itself. If you'd like the package itself to be recorded as well – for example, because the project is deployed as a Shiny application, using an `app.R` that runs an application exported from the package – you can set: Config/renv/snapshot/include-self: TRUE in the package's `DESCRIPTION` file. With this set, the package is also treated as a dependency of the project, and so is expected to be installed in the project library. Note that for the package to be restorable, it should be installed from a remote source – for example, with `renv::install("/")` for a package available on GitHub. The **R** option `renv.snapshot.ignore.self` can also be used to control this behavior: set it to `FALSE` to include the package in the lockfile, or `TRUE` to exclude it. When set, this option takes precedence over the `DESCRIPTION` field. #### See Also More on handling package `dependencies()` Other reproducibility: `lockfiles`, `restore()` #### Examples ``` R ## Not run: # disable automatic snapshots auto.snapshot <- getOption("renv.config.auto.snapshot") options(renv.config.auto.snapshot = FALSE) # initialize a new project (with an empty R library) renv::init(bare = TRUE) # install digest 0.6.19 renv::install("digest@0.6.19") # save library state to lockfile renv::snapshot() # remove digest from library renv::remove("digest") # check library status renv::status() # restore lockfile, thereby reinstalling digest 0.6.19 renv::restore() # restore automatic snapshots options(renv.config.auto.snapshot = auto.snapshot) ## End(Not run) ```"}

### Run an R script

#### Description

It uses the `Rscript` program corresponding to the current R version, to
run the script. It streams `stdout` and `stderr` of the process.

#### Usage

``` R
rscript(
  script,
  cmdargs = character(),
  libpath = .libPaths(),
  repos = default_repos(),
  stdout = NULL,
  stderr = NULL,
  poll_connection = TRUE,
  echo = FALSE,
  show = TRUE,
  callback = NULL,
  block_callback = NULL,
  spinner = FALSE,
  system_profile = FALSE,
  user_profile = "project",
  env = rcmd_safe_env(),
  timeout = Inf,
  wd = ".",
  fail_on_status = TRUE,
  color = TRUE,
  ...
)
```

#### Arguments

|  |  |
|----|----|
| `script` | Path of the script to run. |
| `cmdargs` | Command line arguments. |
| `libpath` | The library path. |
| `repos` | The `repos` option. If `NULL`, then no `repos` option is set. This options is only used if `user_profile` or `system_profile` is set `FALSE`, as it is set using the system or the user profile. |
| `stdout` | Optionally a file name to send the standard output to. |
| `stderr` | Optionally a file name to send the standard error to. It may be the same as `stdout`, in which case standard error is redirected to standard output. It can also be the special string `"2>&1"`, in which case standard error will be redirected to standard output. |
| `poll_connection` | Whether to have a control connection to the process. This is used to transmit messages from the subprocess to the parent. |
| `echo` | Whether to echo the complete command run by `rcmd`. |
| `show` | Logical, whether to show the standard output on the screen while the child process is running. Note that this is independent of the `stdout` and `stderr` arguments. The standard error is not shown currently. |
| `callback` | A function to call for each line of the standard output and standard error from the child process. It works together with the `show` option; i.e. if `show = TRUE`, and a callback is provided, then the output is shown of the screen, and the callback is also called. |
| `block_callback` | A function to call for each block of the standard output and standard error. This callback is not line oriented, i.e. multiple lines or half a line can be passed to the callback. |
| `spinner` | Whether to show a calming spinner on the screen while the child R session is running. By default it is shown if `show = TRUE` and the R session is interactive. |
| `system_profile` | Whether to use the system profile file. |
| `user_profile` | Whether to use the user's profile file. If this is `"project"`, then only the profile from the working directory is used, but the `R_PROFILE_USER` environment variable and the user level profile are not. See also "Security considerations" below. |
| `env` | Environment variables to set for the child process. |
| `timeout` | Timeout for the function call to finish. It can be a base::difftime object, or a real number, meaning seconds. If the process does not finish before the timeout period expires, then a `system_command_timeout_error` error is thrown. `Inf` means no timeout. |
| `wd` | Working directory to use for running the command. Defaults to the current working directory. |
| `fail_on_status` | Whether to throw an R error if the command returns with a non-zero status code. By default no error is thrown. |
| `color` | Whether to use terminal colors in the child process, assuming they are active in the parent process. |
| `...` | Extra arguments are passed to `processx::run()`. |

#### Security considerations

`callr` makes a copy of the user's `.Renviron` file and potentially of
the local or user `.Rprofile`, in the session temporary directory. Avoid
storing sensitive information such as passwords, in your environment
file or your profile, otherwise this information will get scattered in
various files, at least temporarily, until the subprocess finishes. You
can use the keyring package to avoid passwords in plain files."}

### Draw to a PNG file

#### Description

The PNG (Portable Network Graphic) format is one of the most ubiquitous
today, due to its versatiliity and widespread support. It supports
transparency as well as both 8 and 16 bit colour. The device uses
default compression and filtering and will not use a colour palette as
this is less useful for antialiased data. This means that it might be
possible to compress the resulting image even more if size is of concern
(though the defaults are often very good). In contrast to
`grDevices::png()` the date and time will not be written to the file,
meaning that similar plot code will produce identical files (a good
feature if used with version control). It will, however, write in the
dimensions of the image based on the `res` argument.

#### Usage

``` R
agg_png(
  filename = "Rplot%03d.png",
  width = 480,
  height = 480,
  units = "px",
  pointsize = 12,
  background = "white",
  res = 72,
  scaling = 1,
  snap_rect = TRUE,
  bitsize = 8,
  bg
)
```

#### Arguments

|  |  |
|----|----|
| `filename` | The name of the file. Follows the same semantics as the file naming in `grDevices::png()`, meaning that you can provide a `sprintf()` compliant string format to name multiple plots (such as the default value) |
| `width`, `height` | The dimensions of the device |
| `units` | The unit `width` and `height` is measured in, in either pixels (`'px'`), inches (`'in'`), millimeters (`'mm'`), or centimeter (`'cm'`). |
| `pointsize` | The default pointsize of the device in pt. This will in general not have any effect on grid graphics (including ggplot2) as text size is always set explicitly there. |
| `background` | The background colour of the device |
| `res` | The resolution of the device. This setting will govern how device dimensions given in inches, centimeters, or millimeters will be converted to pixels. Further, it will be used to scale text sizes and linewidths |
| `scaling` | A scaling factor to apply to the rendered line width and text size. Useful for getting the right dimensions at the resolution that you need. If e.g. you need to render a plot at 4000x3000 pixels for it to fit into a layout, but you find that the result appears to small, you can increase the `scaling` argument to make everything appear bigger at the same resolution. |
| `snap_rect` | Should axis-aligned rectangles drawn with only fill snap to the pixel grid. This will prevent anti-aliasing artifacts when two rectangles are touching at their border. |
| `bitsize` | Should the device record colour as 8 or 16bit |
| `bg` | Same as `background` for compatibility with old graphic device APIs |

#### Examples

``` R
file <- tempfile(fileext = '.png')
agg_png(file)
plot(sin, -pi, 2*pi)
dev.off()
```"}

+library(readr)

+#' Record the installed dependency closure without activating a project library.
+#'
+#' Run after deliberate dependency changes and rerun the complete test suite.
+#' Uses the caller's configured repositories; does not install/update packages.
+snapshot_population_environment <- function(project_root) {
+  root <- normalizePath(project_root, mustWork = TRUE)
+  dependencies <- readr::read_csv(file.path(root, "config", "dependencies.csv"),
+    col_types = readr::cols(.default = readr::col_character()), show_col_types = FALSE)
+  if (!identical(names(dependencies), c("package", "role")) || !nrow(dependencies) ||

+      any(!nzchar(dependencies$package))) {
+    stop("Dependency manifest must list unique nonempty package names and roles.", call. = FALSE)
+  }
+  renv::snapshot(project = root, packages = dependencies$package,
+                 lockfile = file.path(root, "renv.lock"), prompt = FALSE)
+}

# Posit Assistant Self-Knowledge

## Rules

- **Never speculate** about Posit products or Posit Assistant features.
- **Never provide information** about Posit Assistant without a primary source — either your own system prompt and tool descriptions, the contents of this skill and its reference files, or a linked web page that you have fetched and read.
- Do not invent feature names, pricing details, availability timelines, or configuration options.
- When a linked page covers a topic thoroughly, direct the user there rather than paraphrasing at length.

## Overview

Posit Assistant is a data analysis assistant for RStudio and Positron. It also runs as a standalone web or desktop app, a terminal interface, and a deployable Posit Connect content item. It connects to live R and Python sessions, sees your data, and helps you explore, visualize, build, and debug. It combines conversational AI with code execution and recommends the Posit AI Pass managed service while also supporting direct API keys for other providers.

For questions about using the Positron IDE, Posit Workbench, or Posit Package Manager, or about deploying content to Posit Connect or Posit Connect Cloud, load the `posit-products` skill instead. Its references cover Positron features, panes, interpreters and sessions, troubleshooting, migration, and settings; running IDE sessions in Workbench; Package Manager repositories, snapshots, and configuration; and Connect and Connect Cloud deployment through `rsconnect`, Posit Publisher, and GitHub publishing.

## Posit Assistant Documentation

Primary docs site: https://assistant.posit.co/

### Getting Started

- [Introduction](https://assistant.posit.co/docs/getting-started/) — Installation and first steps
- [Posit AI Pass](https://assistant.posit.co/docs/getting-started/posit-ai/) — Setting up the managed Posit AI Pass service
- [Agent Engines](https://assistant.posit.co/docs/getting-started/agent-engines/) — Connect external agents, authentication, and security limits

### Features

- [Commands](https://assistant.posit.co/docs/features/commands/) — Slash commands (`/plan`, `/clean`, `/report`, `/compact`, etc.)
- [Skills](https://assistant.posit.co/docs/features/skills/) — Built-in and custom skill modules
- [Memory](https://assistant.posit.co/docs/features/memory/) — User-level (`~/.posit/assistant/AGENTS.md`) and project-level (`AGENTS.md`) memory files (general subagents get them; explore and web search subagents don't)
- [Conversations](https://assistant.posit.co/docs/features/conversations/) — History, branching, import/export
- [Plan Mode](https://assistant.posit.co/docs/features/plan-mode/) — Read-only exploration and planning before implementation
- [Chat Features](https://assistant.posit.co/docs/features/chat-features/) — Attachments, thinking effort, web search
- [Context Management](https://assistant.posit.co/docs/features/context-management/) — Token usage, compaction, session context
- [Permissions & Trust](https://assistant.posit.co/docs/features/permissions/) — Approval modes, workspace trust, sandbox
- [Hooks](https://assistant.posit.co/docs/features/hooks/) — Run shell commands at lifecycle events (guardrails, audit logging)

### Guides

- [Explore Your Data](https://assistant.posit.co/docs/guides/explore-your-data/) — Guided EDA walkthrough
- [Build a Dashboard](https://assistant.posit.co/docs/guides/build-a-dashboard/) — Shiny dashboard tutorial

Posit AI Pass service documentation: https://docs.posit.co/posit-ai/

- [Getting Started](https://docs.posit.co/posit-ai/user/getting-started/) — Sign-up and onboarding

# Conversations

Posit Assistant keeps a full history of your conversations. You can switch between them, branch off in new directions, and export conversations in multiple formats.

## Conversation History

All conversations are saved automatically. Use the history panel to:

-   **Switch** between past conversations
-   **Sort** the list by when a conversation was created or by its most recent message, using the sort control under the search box. Your choice is saved as a setting and applies everywhere, including the terminal interface’s conversation picker (press `s` there to switch)
-   **Rename** a conversation to give it a meaningful title (otherwise one is generated automatically)
-   **Delete** conversations you no longer need

![Conversation history panel showing past conversations](/docs/_astro/conversation-history.BmVPoCrl_12sO1G.webp)

## Conversation tabs

Standalone, Desktop, RStudio, and the Positron sidebar can show conversation tabs with the global `features.conversationTabs` setting (`"off"`, `"top"`, or `"side"`; default `"top"`). Changes apply live to running sessions.

Each tab strip can keep up to 12 conversations open. Opening another replaces the currently focused tab but does not delete that conversation. Closing a tab closes only the view: saved history and background work remain available. Deleting a conversation from history is different—it removes that conversation from every open Assistant view.

A conversation that finishes while you are not looking at it shows an unread dot on its tab and history row; choose **Mark as unread** from the tab’s right-click menu or the history row menu to bring the dot back for a conversation you have seen, or **Mark as read** to clear it without opening the conversation.

In Positron, the setting applies to the sidebar and the Assistant window (see below). An Assistant editor panel shows one conversation and never shows a tab strip. To open a conversation in its own editor tab, Cmd/Ctrl+click its row in the conversation history, or choose **Open in new editor tab** from the row menu. Positron then opens a new editor tab in the same editor group. You can split, move, and pin these tabs like any other editor tab. Each tab shows the name of its conversation.

If the conversation is already open in an editor tab, Positron shows that tab instead of opening a second one. **New conversation** in an editor panel replaces the conversation in that panel. To start a fresh conversation in another tab, use the **New Posit Assistant Tab** button in the editor title bar, or run **Posit Assistant: New Editor Tab** from the Command Palette. Closing an editor tab closes only that view.

**Posit Assistant: Open in Editor Tab** (also a button in the sidebar’s title bar) opens the sidebar’s conversation in an editor tab. It leaves the sidebar tab in place, which is useful for viewing the same running analysis beside other work.

To start a new conversation in its own window, run **Posit Assistant: New Window** from the Command Palette. Positron’s **Move into New Window** on an Assistant editor tab moves that conversation into its own window. In recent Positron builds that window shows Posit Assistant’s conversation tabs instead of Positron’s editor tabs, so you can keep several conversations open in it. Its tabs follow `features.conversationTabs`: on the side for `"side"`, and on top for `"top"` or `"off"`. Files you open from that window open in the main Positron window.

In that window, Cmd/Ctrl+click and **Open in new tab** open a conversation in a new tab inside the window. To open one in the main window instead, choose **Open in editor tab** from the history row menu.

## Background notifications

Positron, Standalone, and Desktop can notify you when an unseen background conversation finishes or needs input. Browser permission is requested only from the in-product **Enable notifications** button. Choosing a browser or Positron notification opens the target conversation. Delivery is off by default — turn it on with `features.nativeNotifications` (or `assistant.nativeNotifications` in Positron). RStudio and TUI do not currently deliver native notifications.

## Branching

Conversations in Posit Assistant are stored as a tree, not a flat list. With Assistant’s built-in agent, editing a previous message creates a new branch from that point — your original conversation is preserved alongside the new direction.

With preview [agent engines](/docs/getting-started/agent-engines/), editing and continuing from an earlier turn depend on the engine’s branching capabilities. ACP agents do not support branching at an earlier turn. You can still view saved branches; start a new engine session when continuation is unavailable.

This is useful when you want to:

-   Try a different approach without losing your earlier work
-   Ask the same question in a different way
-   Explore multiple analysis directions from the same starting point

Navigate between branches using the conversation tree controls.

![Conversation branching controls showing navigation between message variants](/docs/_astro/conversation-branching.D7IYfUXn_1JH9J0.webp)

## Import & Export

Export conversations from the **Export / Import** submenu of the overflow menu (gear icon). Available formats:

| Format | Description |
| --- | --- |
| **Markdown** | Plain text export of the conversation. |
| **HTML** | Standalone HTML file that can be viewed in any browser. |
| **JSON** | Full conversation tree structure for programmatic use. |

Conversations can also be imported from previously exported HTML or JSON files, using **Import conversation** in the same submenu.

![Overflow menu with the Export / Import submenu open, showing the export formats and Import conversation](/docs/_astro/export-menu.D0Xx3eoG_Z19Uhd9.webp)

## Token Usage & Compaction

Long conversations accumulate tokens, which affects response quality and speed. With its built-in agent, Posit Assistant manages this automatically:

-   **Auto-compaction** kicks in when the conversation approaches the model’s context limit. The assistant summarizes earlier messages to free up space.
-   **Manual compaction** via [`/compact`](/docs/features/commands/) lets you trigger this yourself. The summary preserves key context while hiding older messages from future requests.
-   **Token counter** — use [`/context`](/docs/features/commands/) to see current token usage.

Compacted messages are never deleted — they’re hidden from the model but preserved in the conversation tree. Previously compacted messages are shown in greyscale.

[Agent engines](/docs/getting-started/agent-engines/) manage their own compaction, and `/compact` is unavailable with them. See [Context Management](/docs/features/context-management/) for engine token reporting and micro-compaction limits.

![Compacted conversation example showing compaction message](/docs/_astro/compact-example.DNJsvEpw_Z2GcY8.webp)

The safest approach is to preserve **the conversation, the project files and a verified backup** separately. None substitutes for the others.

## 1. Export this conversation

In Posit Assistant’s **gear/overflow menu → Export / Import**, export:

| Format | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **JSON** | Preserves the full conversation-tree structure and supports later import |
| **HTML** | Provides a readable standalone copy and also supports import |
| Markdown, optionally | Convenient for searching and quoting in documentation |

Save **both JSON and HTML**. Open the HTML to check it, and ideally test importing the JSON. Don’t assume an export bundles every source file, image or generated output—preserve those separately.

Conversations are saved automatically, but an independent export is a better backup. Official instructions: https://assistant.posit.co/docs/features/conversations/

## 2. Preserve the project—including the outputs

Make a dated archive of the complete [project folder](.), including the original inputs, R scripts, configuration, reference tables, tests, documentation, [renv.lock](renv.lock) and [outputs/](outputs/).

**Important: your project currently has no Git commits, and its files are untracked.** Also, [`.gitignore`](.gitignore) deliberately excludes generated outputs. A Git backup alone would therefore not currently preserve this work, and even after committing it would omit the run evidence unless handled separately.

I recommend committing the reviewed source, tests and documentation to Git, while preserving the generated outputs in the dated archive. Keep a second copy on a separate drive or backed-up storage location.

## 3. Preserve the handover context

Our existing [implementation notes](docs/implementation_progress.md), [test status](docs/test_status.md) and [deployment instructions](docs/deployment.md) capture much of the context. A short handover summary should also identify the selected run, agreed decisions and outstanding validation questions.

There’s no need to rely on saving the entire R session: the scripts and input data can recreate the results. The saved outputs and manifests preserve evidence of what actually ran.

**My recommendation:** JSON + HTML conversation exports, a dated project archive including outputs, and an initial Git commit—then verify a copy opens correctly. Keep these private until you’ve reviewed them for personal paths or other sensitive information.

# Positron IDE commands

These commands act on the Positron workbench itself -- layout, panes, editors,
interpreter sessions, and packages. They do not run interpreter code; use the
tool that runs code in a session for that.

## Calling these commands

Invoke commands with the tool that runs Positron commands, passing the command's
literal `id` exactly as written in the reference files -- copy it, do not retype
it from memory. Where a command takes arguments, fill `args` positionally in the
order given under that command's "Arguments" entry. Omit `args` entirely for commands
that take none -- do not pass an empty object or array. Never invent an argument
value the user hasn't given you or that isn't documented; if a required value is
unknown, ask the user first.

**Find the id here before you run it.** Positron is built on VS Code, so a
plausible-sounding VS Code command id usually does exist and will usually run --
which makes recalling one from memory the most expensive mistake available. Some
ids that read like they do the thing directly instead open a dialog or a
quick-pick and wait for the user to choose, so the command "succeeds" while
handing the task straight back to them. Read the relevant reference file first
and use the id and arguments it gives you. If what the user wants is not covered
by any file below, say so rather than reaching for an id from general VS Code
knowledge.

Some commands take or return an internal id -- a runtime id or a session id.
These are opaque handles you pass back into another command; they are not shown
anywhere in the Positron UI, so a user won't recognize one and it would only
confuse them. Use ids to make the call, but never repeat one to the user. Refer
to a session or interpreter by its name instead.

## When a command doesn't work

- **`disabled`**: the command's precondition doesn't currently hold. Common
  causes are no running interpreter session, or no Data Explorer editor open.
  Report this plainly (e.g. "there's no Data Explorer editor open right now")
  rather than retrying or guessing at a workaround. Each reference file notes
  which of its commands have preconditions.
- **`not-found`**: the command id isn't present in this Positron build, meaning
  the build is older or newer than this skill expects. Report this plainly; do
  not substitute a similarly named id you're unsure about.

## Reference Files

Load the file covering the area in question -- the command ids, arguments, and
return values live there, not in this file.

**UI, layout and panes** -- [references/ui.md](/Users/alex/Library/Application Support/Positron/User/globalStorage/positron.positron-skills/skills/positron-commands/references/ui.md)
Read when the user asks about: switching the workbench layout (four-pane,
notebook, two-pane), bringing a pane into focus (Console, Variables, Help,
Plots, Packages), clearing console output, or expanding/collapsing the Data
Explorer's column summary panel.

**Opening files** -- [references/files.md](/Users/alex/Library/Application Support/Positron/User/globalStorage/positron.positron-skills/skills/positron-commands/references/files.md)
Read when the user wants a file open in Positron: "open data.csv", "show me
that file", "let's look at this CSV/Parquet/Excel file", "browse this JSON
file", or anything that should land in the Data Explorer or Object Explorer.
Read it **before** opening anything -- it documents the commands that open a
known path, and names the similar-looking ids that open a file picker instead
and hand the task back to the user.

**Viewer** -- [references/viewer.md](/Users/alex/Library/Application Support/Positron/User/globalStorage/positron.positron-skills/skills/positron-commands/references/viewer.md)
Read when the user wants to see HTML you have written -- a page, chart, report,
or prototype -- or asks to show a local HTML file or a URL in the Viewer, and
when you need to see or use what's in the Viewer: to check that an app you
started is up and what it shows, or to click, fill in or pick options in an app
the user wants tested. Read it **before** telling the user you can't display
HTML or can't see the Viewer: it documents the commands that show a file or URL
in the Viewer pane, and those that read and use the page there.

**Registered interpreters** -- [references/interpreters.md](/Users/alex/Library/Application Support/Positron/User/globalStorage/positron.positron-skills/skills/positron-commands/references/interpreters.md)
Read when the user asks what interpreters are available or which one the
project uses, wants to install one, says an installed interpreter isn't showing
up, or wants a specific interpreter made available. Also the place to find a
base interpreter before creating an environment.

**Sessions** -- [references/sessions.md](/Users/alex/Library/Application Support/Positron/User/globalStorage/positron.positron-skills/skills/positron-commands/references/sessions.md)
Read when the user asks about: which sessions are running, switching to a
different session, or starting a new one. Also explains the difference between
console sessions and notebook sessions, which decides whether a session can be
selected.

**Stuck sessions and help** -- [references/troubleshooting.md](/Users/alex/Library/Application Support/Positron/User/globalStorage/positron.positron-skills/skills/positron-commands/references/troubleshooting.md)
Read when the user asks about a session that is stuck, needs interrupting, or
needs restarting. Also covers showing a help topic to the user, and reading
installed help and vignettes yourself -- read them before explaining how to use
a function or package, its arguments, or an error it raises.

**Packages** -- [references/packages.md](/Users/alex/Library/Application Support/Positron/User/globalStorage/positron.positron-skills/skills/positron-commands/references/packages.md)
Read when the user asks about: what is installed in a session and at which
version, whether a package is available, out of date or affected by a known
security advisory, or installing and updating packages. Read it **before**

that reports the installed packages, which is always the right way to find out,

Read when the user wants a web app running, stopped or debugged, or asks about

shiny/flask/dash/streamlit/marimo app", "preview my dashboard", "is my app
up?", "what's my app's URL?", "stop the app", "my app is broken", "my app
crashed", "why isn't my app working?". Read it
**before** starting any app server yourself -- app servers must not be started by
running code in a session or a raw terminal command for supported app frameworks. The
commands it documents manage the terminal, detect the app URL, set up any

**Notebooks** -- [references/notebooks.md](/Users/alex/Library/Application Support/Positron/User/globalStorage/positron.positron-skills/skills/positron-commands/references/notebooks.md)
Read when the user wants to create a Jupyter notebook, or read, insert, edit,

**Deploying to Connect** -- [references/publishing.md](/Users/alex/Library/Application Support/Positron/User/globalStorage/positron.positron-skills/skills/positron-commands/references/publishing.md)

87	### `positronPackages.getPackages`
88	
89	Reports **full detail** on the packages you name: the full description plus the
90	detail fields (license, author, source repository, publication date) and the
91	security vulnerabilities that `getAllPackages` leaves out. Pass an array of
92	names (matching is case-insensitive). Use it to look a package up rather than
93	scanning the whole list, and to answer "is X installed?" reliably.
94	
95	**Reading the payload:**
96	
97	- `packages` holds the named packages that **are** installed, with full detail.
98	- `notFound` holds the names that are **not** installed. A name here is a
99	  definitive "not installed" -- that is the reason to name packages rather than
100	  to search the compact list, which can be large.
101	- `metadataStatus` and `vulnerabilityStatus` mean the same as elsewhere (see
102	  above and the advisories section below).
103	- The same `available: false` reasons apply. In addition, if you call it
104	  without any names it returns `reason: 'no-names'` -- pass the package names.
105	
106	**Arguments:**
107	- `names` (array of string): The package names to look up, as the package repository knows them (for example: dplyr, pandas). Pass an array of names, or a single name. Matching is case-insensitive.
108	
109	**Returns:** An object with available: true, the session the packages belong to, packages (the named packages that are installed, with full detail), notFound (the named packages that are not installed -- a name here is a definitive "not installed", not a truncated-away answer), metadataStatus (how the outdated state was obtained: 'fresh', 'cached', 'unsupported', 'timed-out', or 'fetch-failed'), and vulnerabilityStatus (how advisories were obtained). Each installed package carries name, version, latestVersion, outdated, attached, description, url, license, author, sourceRepository, publishedDate, title, and vulnerabilities. vulnerabilities are the security advisories against the installed version, worst first (id, osvId, score, scoreVersion, severity of 'critical'/'high'/'medium'/'low'/'unscored', summary, fixedIn, published, url); an empty array means the repository was asked and reports nothing against that version, which is an all-clear, while an absent field means there is no advisory data for that package at all, which is not. vulnerabilityStatus says how the advisories were obtained: 'fresh' (Package Manager queried now), 'cached' (the cached advisories were still current), 'disabled' (advisory lookups are turned off in settings), 'unavailable' (a lookup ran and produced nothing, which is not worth retrying), or 'timed-out' (the lookup ran out of time partway). vulnerabilitySource names the Package Manager host that served them and when it answered. When no packages are named, an object with available: false and reason 'no-names'. When there are no packages to report at all, an object with available: false and a reason of 'disabled', 'no-session', 'session-not-ready', 'unsupported', or 'failed' -- the last of which also carries a message.

### Compress Files into 'zip' Archives

#### Description

`zip()` creates a new zip archive file.

#### Usage

``` R
zip(
  zipfile,
  files,
  recurse = TRUE,
  compression_level = 9,
  include_directories = TRUE,
  root = ".",
  mode = c("mirror", "cherry-pick")
)

zipr(
  zipfile,
  files,
  recurse = TRUE,
  compression_level = 9,
  include_directories = TRUE,
  root = ".",
  mode = c("cherry-pick", "mirror")
)

zip_append(
  zipfile,
  files,
  recurse = TRUE,
  compression_level = 9,
  include_directories = TRUE,
  root = ".",
  mode = c("mirror", "cherry-pick")
)

zipr_append(
  zipfile,
  files,
  recurse = TRUE,
  compression_level = 9,
  include_directories = TRUE,
  root = ".",
  mode = c("cherry-pick", "mirror")
)
```

#### Arguments

|  |  |
|----|----|
| `zipfile` | The zip file to create. If the file exists, `zip` overwrites it, but `zip_append` appends to it. If it is a directory an error is thrown. |
| `files` | List of file to add to the archive. See details below about absolute and relative path names. |
| `recurse` | Whether to add the contents of directories recursively. |
| `compression_level` | A number between 1 and 9. 9 compresses best, but it also takes the longest. |
| `include_directories` | Whether to explicitly include directories in the archive. Including directories might confuse MS Office when reading docx files, so set this to `FALSE` for creating them. |
| `root` | Change to this working directory before creating the archive. |
| `mode` | Selects how files and directories are stored in the archive. It can be `"mirror"` or `"cherry-pick"`. See "Relative Paths" below for details. |

#### Details

`zip_append()` appends compressed files to an existing 'zip' file.

##### Relative paths

`zip()` and `zip_append()` can run in two different modes: mirror mode
and cherry picking mode. They handle the specified `files` differently.

###### Mirror mode

Mirror mode is for creating the zip archive of a directory structure,
exactly as it is on the disk. The current working directory will be the
root of the archive, and the paths will be fully kept. zip changes the
current directory to `root` before creating the archive.

E.g. consider the following directory structure:

    .
    |-- foo
    |   |-- bar
    |   |   |-- file1
    |   |   `-- file2
    |   `-- bar2
    `-- foo2
        `-- file3

Assuming the current working directory is `foo`, the following zip
entries are created by `zip`:

    setwd("foo")
    zip::zip("../test.zip", c("bar/file1", "bar2", "../foo2"))
    #> Warning in warn_for_dotdot(data$key): Some paths reference parent directory,
    #> creating non-portable zip file
    zip_list("../test.zip")[, "filename", drop = FALSE]
    #> # A data frame: 4 x 1
    #>   filename     
    #>   <chr>        
    #> 1 bar/file1    
    #> 2 bar2/        
    #> 3 ../foo2/     
    #> 4 ../foo2/file3

Note that zip refuses to store files with absolute paths, and chops off
the leading `/` character from these file names. This is because only
relative paths are allowed in zip files.

###### Cherry picking mode

In cherry picking mode, the selected files and directories will be at
the root of the archive. This mode is handy if you want to select a
subset of files and directories, possibly from different paths and put
all of the in the archive, at the top level.

Here is an example with the same directory structure as above:

    zip::zip(
      "../test2.zip",
      c("bar/file1", "bar2", "../foo2"),
      mode = "cherry-pick"
    )
    zip_list("../test2.zip")[, "filename", drop = FALSE]
    #> # A data frame: 4 x 1
    #>   filename  
    #>   <chr>     
    #> 1 file1     
    #> 2 bar2/     
    #> 3 foo2/     
    #> 4 foo2/file3

From zip version 2.3.0, `"."` has a special meaning in the `files`
argument: it will include the files (and possibly directories) within
the current working directory, but **not** the working directory itself.
Note that this only applies to cherry picking mode.

##### Permissions:

`zip()` (and `zip_append()`, etc.) add the permissions of the archived
files and directories to the ZIP archive, on Unix systems. Most zip and
unzip implementations support these, so they will be recovered after
extracting the archive.

Note, however that the owner and group (uid and gid) are currently
omitted, even on Unix.

##### `zipr()` and `zipr_append()`

These function exist for historical reasons. They are identical to
`zip()` and `zipr_append()` with a different default for the `mode`
argument.

#### Value

The name of the created zip file, invisibly.

#### Examples

``` R
## Some files to zip up. We will run all this in the R session's
## temporary directory, to avoid messing up the user's workspace.
dir.create(tmp <- tempfile())
dir.create(file.path(tmp, "mydir"))
cat("first file", file = file.path(tmp, "mydir", "file1"))
cat("second file", file = file.path(tmp, "mydir", "file2"))

zipfile <- tempfile(fileext = ".zip")
zip::zip(zipfile, "mydir", root = tmp)

## List contents
zip_list(zipfile)

## Add another file
cat("third file", file = file.path(tmp, "mydir", "file3"))
zip_append(zipfile, file.path("mydir", "file3"), root = tmp)
zip_list(zipfile)
```"}

+# Preservation, verification and the first Git commit
+
+## What the bundle contains
+
+A dated bundle is created under `preservation/bundles/`. It contains a ZIP,
+detached SHA-256 checksum, per-file checksums, bundle metadata and an extraction
+verification report. The ZIP contains `project/` and `preservation_metadata/`.
+All saved output runs are included despite their Git-ignore rule.
+
+The snapshot deliberately excludes `.git`, local libraries/caches, OS clutter,
+previous bundles and the unrelated personal prompt collection. Exclusions and
+conversation-export presence are recorded. It is not a backup of the running IDE,
+scratch directory or complete Git history. No R workspace dump is required to
+recreate the analysis; historical run artefacts and manifests are retained.
+
+The per-file manifest covers the project payload. It does not hash itself; the
+detached archive checksum covers the ZIP, including its embedded metadata. Hashes
+detect corruption against a trusted reference, not malicious replacement of both
+an archive and all its checksum files. Keep a second copy separately.
+
+## Add and check conversation exports
+
+Follow `docs/conversations/README.md` to save JSON and HTML in that directory.
+Inspect the HTML and test importing the JSON. This manual step is not completed
+by the bundle script. The initial snapshot is explicitly marked pending until
+the files are added; file presence alone still does not prove export completeness.
+
+## Create a new bundle
+
+Source `scripts/create_preservation_bundle.R`, then call
+`create_preservation_bundle(project_root, scratch_directory)` with explicit paths.
+The scratch directory must exist, be writable and be outside the project. The
+tool uses readr, jsonlite, digest and the optional cross-platform zip package;
+their versions are recorded in bundle metadata. The zip package is a preservation
+utility, not a new dependency of the analytical workflow or its existing lockfile.
+No packages are installed or updated automatically.
+
+Each call makes a new UTC-dated output directory. Files are copied to scratch,
+hashed and checked for changes during copying. The ZIP is then extracted into a
+different scratch directory and every project-payload hash is verified. Failure
+does not imply a valid bundle; use only a bundle with a passed verification file.
+Temporary staging/extraction files remain in the supplied scratch area, not in
+the project or analytical outputs.
+
+To verify a copied ZIP, source the same script and call
+`verify_preservation_archive(archive, scratch_directory, expected_sha256)`.
+Use the expected hash from the detached `.sha256` file stored with your trusted
+copy. The function validates archive paths before extracting and checks the
+embedded per-file manifest. Open several important files as an additional check.
+
+The bundler does not execute the analytical workflow, export Assistant history,
+stage files, commit, push, upload, delete or redact anything. A Git commit made
+later is not retroactively part of an older snapshot.
+
+## Review and make the first commit
+
+Use the Positron terminal at the project root. These commands are instructions,
+not actions already performed. First inspect `git status --short`. Review source,
+inputs/licensing, documentation and conversation exports for personal information.
+Do not use `git add .`: it would risk adding unrelated personal files.
+
+After reviewing, stage only the intended project files:
+
+```sh
+git add .gitignore README.md renv.lock run_population.R Inputs R scripts config reference tests docs
+git diff --cached --stat
+git diff --cached --check
+git status --short
+```
+
+`docs/` includes the conversation exports once added. Include them only after
+privacy review. Outputs and dated bundles remain ignored and are preserved by
+the ZIP instead. `Useful prompts.txt` should remain untracked unless you make a
+separate explicit decision to include it. No remote repository is configured by
+these commands.
+
+When the staged selection is correct:
+
+```sh
+git commit -m "Preserve reviewed population workflow and handover"
+git log -1 --oneline
+git status --short
+```
+
+If Git requests your identity, set your chosen name/email for this repository
+using local configuration; do not invent an identity or change global settings
+without deciding to do so. A successful local commit is not an off-machine
+backup. Use approved private remote storage or another protected backup copy.
+
+After the commit, make another dated bundle so its metadata records the commit
+hash. It still excludes Git internals/history: back up the repository separately,
+for example with an approved private remote, if retaining Git history is required.
